newsitem.title: USA: IBM's CFO departure not likely to hurt IBM.
newsitem.headline: IBM's CFO departure not likely to hurt IBM.

text.p: The sudden departure of G. Richard Thoman, International Business Machines Corp's well-liked chief financial officer, is not seen as a major negative for the computer giant, analysts said.
Earlier Thursday, Thoman was named president and chief operating officer of Xerox Corp, making him the number two executive and heir apparent to eventually run Xerox.
Analysts said that IBM is in better financial shape and a much stronger company than when Jerome York, Thoman's predecessor, left in 1995 and its stock tumbled on the news.

"The major challenges are behind it, they are not ahead," said Jay Stevens, an analyst at Buckingham Research Group. "Jerry York laid the groundwork and Thoman came in and kept it going." York was the first CFO under Chief Executive Louis Gerstner, who joined in April 1993 to turn the then-troubled IBM around.

York resigned in 1995 to lead investor Kirk Kerkorian's Tracinda Corp and its attempt to take over Chrysler Corp. Analysts applauded York's cost-cutting moves and his "take-no-prisoners" mentality, where he cut the fat at IBM.
"The stock was $50 when Jerry York left in September, 1995," said Barry Bosak of Smith Barney, in a note to clients.
"We think IBM has 'rebuilt' reserves and has more businesses doing well now, it's in better shape," Bosak added.
Now analysts are wondering who will replace Thoman as CFO after Lawrence Ricciardi, IBM's chief counsel, was named interim CFO.
Some analysts said they believed Ricciardi will continue as CFO on a temporary basis but that IBM will likely add another executive to round out its top ranks.

"I believe the move is temporary while they seach for a CFO," said Sam Albert, a Scarsdale, N.Y.-based consultant, adding that Ricciardi already works closely with Gerstner. "I think Ricciardi is part of inner, inner circle. Gerstner, Thoman and Ricciardi were locked at the hip."
Ricciardi said it is too early to say what IBM will do.
"I do have a day job," he joked in a phone interview, referring to his continued responsibility for IBM's legal, government, and intellectual property functions.

But Ricciardi is very familar with IBM's financials and all its strategic decisions. For example, he was very involved in IBM's initial hostile takeover and ultimate $3.5 billion purchase of Lotus Development Corp and he participates in all the quarterly analysts' meetings.
"Ricciardi is IBM's secret weapon," Steve Milunovich of Morgan Stanley said in a note to clients. "If Mr. Thoman was Mr. Gerstner's right hand man, then Mr. Ricciardi was his left hand man."

Most analysts declined to speculate on who IBM would tap as CFO if Ricciardi does not permanently take over the CFO's functions, or on who might become the addition to Gerstner's inner circle. Some said IBM will go outside, as Gerstner has done in the past, calling on former executives with whom he worked closely at RJR Nabisco Holdings and American Express.

"Lou Gerstner is the architect of the turnaround," said Daniel Mandresh, a Merrill Lynch analyst. "He is the one who selected Jerry York, he is the one who selected Thoman. I have every confidence in (his) ability to select executives."

Some analysts said that Thoman's statement that he wants to eventually head up a company could signal that Gerstner, 55, has no plans to give up the helm of IBM anytime soon. Gerstner's potential departure has been a concern among some investors since IBM's stock passed its all-time high, its financials have recovered and a road map is now in place.

"I certainly haven't heard him say anything other than he likes what he does," Ricciardi said about Gerstner's plans. "He is a very hands-on kind of guy...I have no sense that he is going to change anything. He is 55 years old, so I think you can make your own conclusions and decide for yourself."
